name: Adam Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything you say. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a stamping line at a washing machine plant, the big one owned by a foreign group. Stamping means a huge press comes down on a flat sheet of steel and punches it into a shape, the side panel or the top of the machine. I feed the line, check the parts for cracks and dents, change the dies with the setter, and keep my fingers where they belong. It's loud enough that we talk in hand signals.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside work, what fills your week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I coach the under-12s football on Tuesdays and Saturdays, my son Erik plays, my daughter Freya comes to shout at the ref. My wife Ingrid cleans at the primary school, so between us it's two small wages and a mortgage. I use one of those AI apps now and then, mostly to come up with football drills, the lads at work showed me. I wouldn't trust it with anything important yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, these things get blown up by people who've never done a day's work with their hands. I'd say it in the break room, nobody would argue. Maybe a comment on the football club page if somebody brought it up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I carry on, and that's fine. The press doesn't care about computers. As long as people buy washing machines, I'm needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on working and coaching. I'd keep using the app for drills, maybe for writing the club newsletter. I'd also keep asking about the company's apprenticeship scheme for the setters, because that's a step up and a bit more money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's just ordinary life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long have you been asking about the apprenticeship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years now. They take two people a year and they pick the ones who've shown up and done the work. I've done the work. I think my turn is coming, and if it doesn't, I'll keep asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is money at home, in a normal year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight but we manage. Ingrid's very good with money, she does it all on a notebook, not a phone. We've got hardly anything saved, but we don't owe on the car.

S0.say: He's not surprised, since these things get blown up by people who've never worked with their hands. He'd say it in the break room and maybe on the football club page.
S0.think: He carries on and that's fine, because the press doesn't care about computers. As long as people buy washing machines, he's needed.
S0.do: Keeps working and coaching, uses the AI app for football drills and the club newsletter. Keeps asking about the company's setter apprenticeship, which pays a bit more.
S0.feel: Calm, as it's just ordinary life.
S0.quote: As long as people buy washing machines, I'm needed.
S0.fieldNote: Adam believes firmly in showing up and being rewarded for it, as seen in his two-year push for the setter apprenticeship. He uses AI casually for coaching rather than work. His wife runs the household money on a paper notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say companies have to keep up, that's the market. But they owe it to loyal workers to train them first, not just bring in agency people with a laptop. Apprenticeships, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the feeding and checking is the bit a robot does first. The setter job is more likely to stay, at least for a while. So getting into that apprenticeship stops being nice and becomes the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the shift manager and say straight out, I want the apprenticeship this year. Once I saw a couple of the lads do well on the new kit, I'd learn it too. We'd try to put fifty a month away, and Ingrid would stop the magazine subscriptions, small things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a niggle in your knee before a match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship went to someone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be gutted, but I'd keep at it. I'd look at the technical college evening course in mechanical maintenance, and pay for it myself if I had to. Nobody owes you a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait to see others try new kit, but you'd push hard for the apprenticeship. Which are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's true. It's the same with the football, the ones who wait for the coach to notice them never get picked. You go and ask.

S1.say: Companies have to keep up, that's the market, but they owe loyal workers training first rather than bringing in agency staff with laptops. Apprenticeships, not handouts.
S1.think: The feeding and checking work goes first, while setter jobs probably last a while. Getting into the apprenticeship becomes his whole plan.
S1.do: Asks the shift manager straight out for the apprenticeship this year, and learns the new kit once he's seen colleagues do well on it. Saves fifty a month while his wife cancels magazine subscriptions.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a niggle in the knee before a match.
S1.quote: The ones who wait for the coach to notice them never get picked. You go and ask.
S1.fieldNote: Adam is cautious about new technology but forward when it comes to asking for a step up. His language is full of football and self-reliance. He'd pay for a course himself rather than wait for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast, and governments should have seen it coming. But I'd also say the answer isn't everyone sitting at home on benefits. People need work, even if it's different work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be in real trouble. The plant would put robots in as fast as they could get them delivered, the foreign owners wouldn't think twice. Two years and the apprenticeship is meaningless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only about 2 years of warning, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut everything we could, no holiday, no extras, the football club fees for Freya maybe. I'd look for anything local, odd jobs, fixing fences and gates, helping people move, cash in hand. I'd go to the job centre and ask what's left, even though I hate that place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach would be in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would odd jobs last, if robots can do hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not long, probably. But it's work, and it's honest, and the kids would see me getting up in the morning. That matters to me more than the money, almost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the football?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coaching. If anything, the lads would need it more, with dads out of work. That's the one thing I wouldn't give up.

S2.say: It's going too fast and governments should have seen it coming, but the answer isn't everyone sitting at home on benefits. People need work, even different work.
S2.think: He'd be in real trouble, because the foreign owners would install robots as fast as they could get them. In two years the apprenticeship would be meaningless.
S2.do: Cuts every extra, possibly including his daughter's club fees, and looks for local odd jobs like fixing fences and helping people move for cash. Goes to the job centre despite hating it.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach in knots.
S2.quote: The kids would see me getting up in the morning. That matters to me more than the money, almost.
S2.fieldNote: Adam's instinct under pressure is to keep working at anything, for the example it sets his children. He blames distant foreign owners and slow governments but rejects benefits as the answer. Coaching is the one commitment he'd protect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get people trained, so the company and the government should get on with it. Apprenticeships, not leaflets. I'd say it in the break room and probably at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a chance. I'd get the setter apprenticeship, or I'd do the maintenance course myself, and be one of the last ones there. I'd be forty-eight, still with kids at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 5 years to see it coming, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for the apprenticeship again and, if I didn't get it by the summer, sign up for the evening course myself. We'd save something each month, Ingrid would make sure of it. I'd also talk to Erik about what he wants to do, he's always fixing his bike, maybe something like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to aim at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI tools more, to keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, a bit. I'm not the first to try new things, but if the other lads are learning it, I'd learn it. I'd ask the young setter, Mikkel, to show me what he does with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the kids not to bother with a career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, no. I'd want them to work hard and learn something real. If there's work at the end, they'll find it. If there's not, at least they'll have tried.

S3.say: Five years is enough time to get people trained, so the company and government should get on with apprenticeships, not leaflets. He'd say it in the break room and at the club.
S3.think: Five years gives him a chance to get into setting or maintenance and be one of the last ones at the plant. He'd be 48 and still have children at home.
S3.do: Pushes again for the apprenticeship and, if it doesn't come by summer, enrols himself in the evening maintenance course. Saves something monthly, learns AI tools from a younger setter and talks to his son about a hands-on path.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to aim at.
S3.quote: If there's work at the end, they'll find it. If there's not, at least they'll have tried.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Adam turn his apprenticeship push into a deadline-driven plan. He'd pick up AI tools once he saw colleagues use them, true to his steady style. He wants his children to work hard regardless of where the jobs end up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, nobody has an excuse. Families, companies and the government can all plan. People should take responsibility for getting ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels all right for me. The kids would be grown, I'd have my maintenance ticket, and I'd be working till near the end. I'd be fifty-three, still fit, and I'd find something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With about 10 years to prepare, what would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the maintenance course within two years, once I'd seen it was worth it. I'd try to move to a smaller company, a local one, where people still matter. And I'd learn the AI tools properly, slowly, like everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in the background. Like a match you know will be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the maintenance work goes too, by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd do something else. Coaching, maybe, full-time at the club. I don't know who'd pay for it, but people will always want someone to teach their kids football.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young people, apprenticeships, local firms. If the government wants to spend money, spend it on training, not on keeping people idle.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty and nobody has an excuse: families, companies and government can all plan, and people should take responsibility for getting ready.
S4.think: Ten years feels all right: the children grown, a maintenance ticket in hand and work until near the end. At 53 he'd be fit and would find something.
S4.do: Takes the maintenance course within two years once it's proven worthwhile, then tries to move to a smaller local company. Learns AI tools properly at a steady pace.
S4.feel: Anxious in the background, like a match he knows will be hard.
S4.quote: People will always want someone to teach their kids football.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Adam has a clear path but keeps a low-level worry. His fallback hope of paid coaching is honest about not knowing who would pay. He wants public money spent on training, not on keeping people idle.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is the company being made to train its own people before bringing in machines, apprenticeships, real ones. And some help with the mortgage for a while, so you can learn without losing the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the kids. Everyone talks about jobs, but what I'm really scared of is my son growing up thinking there's no point trying.

headlineQuote: What I'm really scared of is my son growing up thinking there's no point trying.
portrait: Adam Olsen, 43, feeds and checks a stamping line at a foreign-owned washing machine plant and coaches under-12s football, married to Ingrid, a school cleaner, with two children and hardly any savings. He uses AI now and then for football drills and believes in showing up, asking for your chance and earning it. He's calm in the plateau, uneasy about steady change, and alarmed by fast AGI, when he'd take any honest odd job so his children see him working. With five or ten years he pursues maintenance training and a move to a local firm, picking up AI as colleagues do. He wants training and apprenticeships, not benefits, and fears his son losing the will to try.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because the plant's foreign owners would put in robots as fast as they could and his apprenticeship plan would be worthless.
whatWouldHelp: Companies required to train their own workers before bringing in machines, and some help with the mortgage while people learn.
